speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I shall endeavour, as soon after the house reconvenes as possible, to make known to hon. members the measures the government will introduce. In the very nature of things there is no effort to delay the introduction of legislation, but the two bills now before the committee on banking and commerce involve legislation in connection with at least three other matters, and until such time as they are disposed of the legislation cannot be submitted to the house. I have no doubt the right hon. gentleman knows how difficult it is to get all persons interested at one time to consider and to deal with matters of public importance. subtopic: REPORT OF INQUIRY CONDUCTED BY HON. DONALD SUTHERLAND
speechtext:
The report to which reference was made is the report of a commissioner-not a royal commissioner-made under the Combines Investigation Act. In the past it has not been the practice nor has it been considered advisable to make these reports public. Section 28 of the Combines Investigation Act which deals with the publicity which should be given to reports is as follows:
Any report of a commissioner, other than an interim report, shall within fifteen days after its receipt by the minister be made public, unless the commissioner is of the opinion that the public interest would be better served by withholding publication and so states in the report itself, in which case the minister may exercise his discretion as to the publicity to be given to the report in whole or in part.
2. The minister may publish and supply copies of any report in such manner and upon such terms as to him seems most desirable.
This section refers to a commissioner under the act. Then, section 27 deals with the report of the registrar, and is silent as to publication. However, heretofore the practice has been that those reports are not made public. The reason obviously is that when the registrar makes an investigation by himself or by one appointed for such purposes, all the persons or firms are inquired into ex parte, and the information is given in confidence. The act contemplates that any six persons, by signing an application and without stating anything further than that in their opinion a combine exists, may start the machinery in motion. This proceeding is not like other quasi criminal or criminal matters where informations are laid and where the informant must, as in the case of a search warrant, state the reasons upon which his belief is founded. Very frequently it happens, at least so I am told by those who have been associated with the operation of the act for years, that where the six persons sign the application they do not appear as witnesses at all. It is sufficient to start the law in motion merely to state that in the opinion of the six a combine exists. The registrar then investigates. The registrar on an ex parte investigation may conclude that a com-

Tobacco Industry
bine in restraint of trade, a combine as interpreted by the act, does exist, but up to that time the investigation is still ex parte in a sense, the persons being investigated giving the details of their business to the registrar. But, as in this case, where the registrar in the exercise of his discretion says that in his opinion a combine does not exist it would be unfair, and I think the practice heretofore followed is sound, that the confidential information incorporated in the report of the registrar should be made available to the competitors of the firm or firms whose business was being investigated.
The investigation by the registrar, if further proceedings are taken, becomes the foundation ultimately of a criminal prosecution. The nesxt step would be the review by the minister of the registrar's decision if he has declared that the act has been violated, and then those whose conduct is under review, so far as I have been able to learn, do not appear before the minister whether he may or may not agree with the registrar, although I think it has rarely happened that the minister has disagreed with the registrar.
If a combine is reported to be in existence, the record then goes to the appropriate attorney general, or it may be referred to a royal commission, and the royal commissioner may then conduct an inquiry in public. That is the publicity that is referred to in section 28. He may report that the firms have been guilty of an invasion of the act. But during all these various investigations there has been no charge laid. The people are not put upon their trial. Their business is simply being investigated. Ultimately, as I say, the report may be dispatched to the appropriate attorney general of the province in which the offence is said to have occurred, and it is there reviewed by the law officers of the province, because the province is charged, under our constitution, with the administration of these statutes. They may conclude that there is no offence. If they so conclude, in the face of the registrar's decision and possibly the decision of a royal commissioner, that a violation of the act has taken place, then after the lapse of three months a prosecution may take place at the instance of the attorney general for Canada. But up to that point the people whose conduct is under review have never been charged with an offence, and it is not until they come before a magistrate in the province and a charge is laid and a preliminary inquiry held that the
necessity for making out a prima facie case sufficient to put a person upon his trial arises. If a prima facie case is made out the person may be tried before the magistrate or, having the right of election, may go up for trial to the next court having competent jurisdiction, and in the usual course an indictment would be laid before the grand jury. There might even then be no bill found. If a true bill is found, then for the first time the person comes before the courts to have his conduct with respect to non-compliance with the provisions of the Combines Act brought under the review of the tribunal which would impose a penalty if a verdict of guilty was returned.
So it will be seen that during the course of the proceedings under the Combines Act, if the inquiries made by the registrar were made public, the person whose conduct was under review might suffer a very great injury, and particularly so when the registrar's report is to the effect that no combine within the meaning of the act exists, because it is obvious that the information gathered by him and by his officers, being in many instances of a confidential nature, would then immediately become known to the man's competitors. As I say, the practice in the past in this house, so far as I have been able to learn, has been not to make these reports public, and I agree with the established practice. If, for instance, the committee at present sitting on price spreads desires to have the position of the growers of tobacco spread upon the record-

grain, all operating under this act, are to my mind entirely foreign to relief. It might be said that the loan to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company for the purpose of employing men might well be included. But surely where guarantees are of such a wide and varied character as those indicated by the minister in his report of the orders in council passed under the legislation, the government of Canada is becoming responsible for a staggering amount in the event of failure of payment; and, frankly, with respect to some of these investments the government will more than likely have to come to the rescue. Omnibus legislation of this kind is very unsatisfactory. If the government wants to take to itself power to help Canadian financial institutions it ought to bring in a measure taking power to help those institutions but it should not do so in this back door sort of way.
In connection with relief proper I have a suggestion to offer to the government. This is the last day before we adjourn for Easter recess. It is quite obvious that before we adjourn we cannot get very far in legislation of this kind. Further, as was announced yesterday, the meeting which was to have taken place between the provinces and the Dominion government has been postponed for some time. We cannot intelligently discuss this matter until we have the report as to the arrangements that are likely to be made between the provinces and the Dominion government. Members of every party in the house are quite willing that relief shall be granted and are anxious that a proper relief scheme should be inaugurated, but as matters stand now, we are inevitably thrown into hostile camps and either we have to defend a policy that is not very clear or oppose one about which we know and can know very little. My suggestion is that the government should not press this matter to-day, but rather, during the recess, should take into serious consideration the drafting of a constructive program designed to deal with the whole unemployment situation. We have been promised in the past that the government would seriously consider some sort of unemployment insurance scheme. We have been promised that they would inaugurate some sort of public works scheme. We have been told that the present scheme of the dole is very unsatisfactory. I think the Prime Minister believes that; I think we all believe it. It was initiated two years ago as a sort of stop-gap arrangement and it would seem as if we should not indefinitely carry on along this line.
I should like to give the government credit for two measures that they have brought down this session. First, the central bank arrangement, which, although I do not altogether like the details of it, is one that shows a great deal of boldness and imagination and marks a distinctly forward step. Again, while I do not wrant to anticipate the discussion on the marketing legislation, I concede that it also has boldness and imagination. The government in these two very important departments of our public life is preparing to take a really forward step. I would venture to suggest that they might very well bring forward a third measure dealing with unemployment. Then side by side with the central bank and marketing legislation, rounding out, as it were, their program we would have a well conceived and carefully drafted bill dealing with this important question of unemployment. It is quite obvious that the government have been influenced in their central bank legislation by some of the developments in Great Britain, the United States and elsewhere, and that also in their marketing legislation they have been influenced by developments in the United States, Great Britain and some of the other dominions. I cannot see why they should not receive whatever help they can from the NRA and from some of the schemes that have been put into operation in Great Britain, and bring in this session a carefully arranged scheme. I believe such a scheme would be fairly well assured of support on the part of this house. I cannot speak for the official opposition, but I think I can speak more or less for members in our own corner, and more than that, for a very large number of people throughout the country. If I read the press aright, I think the public generally expect the government to do something of this kind. I am not particularly concerned with the political future of the government, but even from that standpoint they would be well advised, when they are looking after the financial and commercial interests, not to neglect labour and those who at one time were in the ranks of labour but who to-day are in the ranks of the unemployed. This session would not be altogether barren if the government would carefully consider such a suggestion and bring in a definite scheme.

One notices in the press that Beauharnois is making a new issue of bonds and I assumed the moneys were perhaps to be devoted towards discharging the liability to the banks by whom the money was advanced. I am not usually very critical of some of the acts of the government, perhaps not so much as I should be; I like to be on pretty safe ground when I do offer any criticism. Certainly no one on this side of the house, I believe, has any fault to find if the government uses the authority which it has for the purpose of relieving those who ire unemployed. But I cannot see how the government possibly can bring under the category of relief to the unemployed such matters as to the guarantee of $60,000,000 to the Canadian Pacific, for example. That has not the remotest connection with unemployment or unemployment relief. Neither, I think, has the making of loans to the various provinces to the extent of something like $52,000,000. Certainly it can have no possible connection with relief when we guarantee the debts of the Dominion of Newfoundland, or what now has become the colony of Newfoundland. As I recall it the only excuse given for joining with Great Britain in guaranteeing Newfoundland's debts was that it might tend to destroy or hurt the credit of Canada if Newfoundland went into default. I think that is so far fetched, Mr. Chairman, as not to be worth any consideration whatsoever. Thus, by way of guarantees to the Canadian Pacific and to the Beauharnois company; by way of gifts to certain industrial concerns such as the Dominion Steel, the Algoma Steel and the Canadian Pacific; by way of loans and guarantees and advances we have committed ourselves to something like $100,000,000 or $125,000,000, a tremendous sum.
As I say, Mr. Chairman, I have no objection whatever to having those powers used for the legitimate purpose of relieving unemployment, but as I said before I do not see how you can possibly argue that such a thing as the guarantee of the loan to the Canadian Pacific or the guarantee of the. debts of the colony of Newfoundland possibly coidd come in that category. If these things are done-and in this connection I refer also to the loans made to the provinces, in connection with which I am not sure that we ought to go any further-is it not just conceivable that the credit of the Dominion of Canada will be affected fully as much as if some of these corporations or provinces were allowed to go into default?
I arose more particularly, perhaps, to criticize the method by which the government 
guaranteed the advance to the Canadian Pacific. I hope no one will think I have any particular prejudice towards that great company, but I do say, as the leader of the opposition said a few days ago, that it should not have been done under this aet; it has no connection whatever with relief. If it were thought desirable-and I think it is highly questionable whether or not it was desirable *-to guarantee the $60,000,000 loaned by the banks to the Canadian Pacific against the retirement of their bonds, it should not have been done in the way it was done. The matter should have been brought to parliament and parliament should have passed upon it. I think it was almost an affront to this house and to hon. members, in view of the fact that parliament was in session last year at the time negotiations were being carried on in connection with this guarantee of $60,000,000, that parliament was not advised of what was taking place. I will say this, also; when it was definitely decided that the guran-tee should be made, with this house in session I say it was almost an affront to this parliament that due notice was not given to that effect. If we are to continue in that way where in the world will we end? I leave it to the fair minded members on the other side of the house as to whether or not this sort of thing should be carried on indefinitely. If it was right to guarantee the $60,000,000 loan to the Canadian Pacific for the retirement of their obligations surely it was the privilege of hon. members of this house to know about it when we were actually in session at the time.
I rise now to make my protest against that sort of thing; I think it should not be countenanced, and I believe if hon. members opposite had their say they would disapprove of it also.

Dear Sir,-
Your letter of the 9th was received to-day, tor which I thank you sincerely and appreciate yenr kindly interest.
The strike, which is directly responsible for the peculiar position of the striking bushmen here took place on the fifteenth of January. It was due to the unrest and dissatisfaction of years, culminating in the extremely bad conditions this year. The principal points of contention were low wages, long hours and unsanitary living conditions.
The monthly wage rate on the limits of Austin and Nicholson was on a sliding scale of $15 to $26 per month so that a man never could find out his rate until he was being paid off, and then it was at the discretion of the foreman. Work by the month was difficult to obtain because it was an advantage to the lumber company to have the men cutting on a

piecework basis. The price, per double cord of spruce pulp, varied from two dollars to three dollars, and again nothing was definite till the pay-off. The bush was exceedingly poor, for seven of the eight camps in operation on the Jack Pine river were working in old cuts, that had already been worked for three to five years previously. The bush was full of old jack pine slash and tops from previous log cutting operations and the men had to cut their way through this in order to clean out the spruce that was left. Very few spruce swamps remained that had not been cut through before. Only one new camp was in a fresh cut. The "cord" required was of oversize dimensions and measured 8 feet, 4 inches by 8 feet 4 inches by 4 feet 4 inches, and on the strips the cutter had to cut his orvn road ten to twelve feet wide. During the early part of the season the Department of Lands and Forests cut eighty cents per double cord off the timber dues, payable to the department by the company, for the express purpose of that eighty cents being passed on to the men in extra wages, but the men never received the eighty-cent increase, and therefore decided that the company kept the sum as found money. The most difficult sections of the bush were let out to sub-jobbers who erected miserable shacks and tried to grind a profit out of the hard-working pieceworkers by paying the wretched minimum wage.
The measuring and culling, according to which the men were paid, was done by the camp clerk though there were government scalers, Abitibi scalers and company sealers and cheek scalers in the camps. The men went out to their work in the dark of the morning and did not return to camp till the dusk of evening in a vain attempt to earn a living wage. In many of the camps the average walk to and from work was from one to three miles.
The food was comparatively abundant for the simple reason that even a steam boiler must be stoked with sufficient fuel to give pressure enough to do the job. It is the unwholesomeness of the food that is the chief complaint, for often the beans and potatoes are served sour, owing to being cooked over and over again. Another glaring example of the disregard for the men's stomachs is the fact that sugar was sent out to the bush for the noon lunch in an umvashed lye can as a container. All the grievances cannot be mentioned here but merely a few that are representative of the many.
Then comes the passage that I quoted in the house on Monday last regarding the deplorable conditions of the blankets issued to the men. The letter continues on page 5 as follows:
The law prescribes certain facilities for washing and drying of clothing. At Gray's camp the facilities provided consisted of two empty lard cans for heating of water and one washtub and washboard for over one hundred men, and the washing was done on the edge of the manure heap between the barn and the river. The men were not permitted to do washing in the camp, while the building constructed in lieu of a wash shack was converted into living quarters for the foreman and his wife.

Men arriving at Nicholson Siding to go into the camps slept over night in the bunkhouse there, which is under control of G. B. Nicholson, and required to sleep in dirty blankets there, invariably became infested with vermin and therefore carried vermin into the camps where, owing to the wooden construction of the bunks and unwashed blankets, conditions can only be described as terrible.
There were no dry rooms in the camps and as a result of wet shirts, socks and boots drying around the bunkhouse stoves at night, the breathing atmosphere was contaminated with steam and foul odour. The floors were not kept clean, no cuspidor of any type existed on the camp floors and the towelling was not sufficient nor kept in a sanitary condition. If only the existing sanitary law's were enforced all this could not be possible.
As a result of the foregoing genuine grievances a strike was organized with the assistance of some members of the Lumber Workers' Industrial Union of Canada who v'ere working in the camps at the time. The majority of the men in the camps quit work of their own free will on January 15 and walked to the headquarters camp where they congregated and held the first strike meeting. At this meeting a strike committee and executive were democratically elected from members of the camps present to represent all the different types of work and nationalities. The committee in session appointed Davis and Berry,-

William Austin, a junior member of the firm of Austin and Nicholson was at the camp that day so he was immediately approached by a delegation of three of the workers in an attempt on our part for strike settlement. William Austin claimed to have authority to settle the affair in the interests of the company, so he was presented with a list of the grievances and demands, and time was allowed him for consideration. In this interval two provincial police arrived at the headquarters camp. G. B. Nicholson had been informed of the impending strike on the previous day and had immediately gone to Toronto to interview the Attorney General and General Williams and, according to reports, had been promised there enough provincial police, man for man if necessary, to counterbalance the strikers. About four o'clock on the afternoon of January 15, William Austin came into the main bunkhouse of the headquarters camp, together with two Ontario provincial police, and told the men that he could not meet their demands, said the wage scale would remain the same as on January 1 and as for shorter hours and better conditions he said he would do his best, conceding that board charges and price of van goods were too high. This was considered as no strike
settlement, so the strikers were informed that they were fired and were asked to draw their time and leave the camps. The strikers decided then to make strike headquarters in Chapleau, where the only representative of law and order in the immediate unorganized district was stationed permanently, namely, the district provincial police officer, P. Boland. The strikers were advised by me, as picket captain, to conduct themselves as respectable citizens, to break none of the laws and to use no force in an attempt to have other workers join our cause, other than merely explaining the situation and asking them to join us. This has been the system of picketing to date, and as a result not one man, to my knowledge, has been arrested because of his strike activities. Approximately four hundred men came out on strike. Approximately one hundred remained in the camps as camp foremen, clerks, scalers, some teamsters and personal friends of the staff who were working in the camps.
In the thirty mile walk from the camps to the Canadian Pacific railroad at Nicholson Siding the men suffered hardship of cold and some walking through the night, but all arrived at the bunkhouse at the siding which was thrown open to us by the provincial police ais shelter. The police were fair in assuming a neutral position and also made arrangements to have our baggage safely transferred from headquarters camp to Chapleau. On January 17 about three hundred strikers bought tickets and travelled by train to Chapleau while a number walked the 22 miles in order to save the 85 cents for food when arrived in Chapleau. Several men remained at Nicholson Siding as a picket guard to explain the situation to any strike breakers that might be shipped in, but these men were forced to leave the siding owing to Nicholson enforcing a "no trespassing" order.
In Chapleau the strikers shared their meagre funds with each other, as the majority of them were figured out "in the hole" by the camp clerks. Also assistance in the way of cash came in from affiliated union organizations in Sudbury, Port Arthur, Sault Ste. Marie, Timmins, Toronto, and other centres where hushmen, miners and industrial workers were in sympathy with our clean fight for a living wage, shorter hours and sanitary living conditions. In these centres the workers established picket lines to page the employment offices and notify anyone hiring for jobs with Austin and Nicholson of the strike conditions that existed here. The strike received publicity in all the chief newspapers in Sudbury, Ottawa, Toronto and other centres.
We sent a deputation to the town council of Chapleau to explain our position in the municipality, as an organized body of citizens coming in from the unorganized districts in the vicinity in order to arrange for settlement of an industrial dispute or strike. We explained that as an organized body we were in a position to care for ourselves, keep order among our members and respect the rights of the citizens of the municipality. The town fathers offered us their cooperation on behalf of Chapleau, and we arranged to get the use of the municipal hall for a meeting place on January 18 in order to get all the strikers together from all the camps for the first time, and discuss the situation and grievances in order to draw up

This list of demands was handed to G. B. Nicholson on January 20 by myself together with two fellow strikers, Fred Wright and J. St. Micheal in the presence of two provincial police. Nicholson told us he would give us bis reply via provincial police at two p.m. that afternoon. At three p.m. the strikers assembled in the hall and considered Nicholson's declaration. He said, according to script transferred by him, that the wages would remain as on January I and that his camps would continue to be run in a clean and satisfactory manner as had always been their practice, at least this was the gist of it. Needles to say the assembled strikers voted unanimously to reject Nicholson's proposal as a strike settlement, as we con-
sidered it an insult to our intelligence. We decided to carry on the strike.
Nicholson was furious and called a meeting (public) in the town hall on January 22 where be reviled the town council for assisting a "soviet led group of people," as such he slanderously referred to we strikers in breaking down his ultra-honest business, and made personal remarks which he was forced to retract later in the press. His meeting was not an orderly one and instead of gaining public sympathy, the tendency was to destroy what little he had previously. It was merely a publicity stunt for his own publication in the press.
At this time Nicholson was resorting to despicable methods to break our strike. Men were forced off relief in outside centres of Ontario and shipped to Nicholson, being told the strike was settled. One of these men, Albert Viauzin of Blind River, told me personally of these conditions. Also a number of men from Gracefield, in the province of Quebec, were shipped in as strikebreakers under a heavy guard of C.R.R. and provincial police. Ihis, in my mind, is forced labour and synonymous with slavery, against which our ancestors fought and bled, and now it is here again in the year of 1934. The camps were filled by false pretences and force, and thereby our jobs were taken from us.
By January 24, our funds were depleted to such aii extent that we were unable to buy sufficient food supplies to furnish the two feed camps, which we had established to feed our men en masse, two meals a day. As a result we made application to T. H. Wolfe, District lyeliet Officer, tor relief in the matter of food, cioth:ng and shelter, which we claimed to be entitled to, as respectable citizens of Ontario, who had helped to build up the relief funds from which we wished to draw. On January 25 we made formal application and declared destitute in a registration the number of 251 men. Hie wage scale notice which accompmi s this letter was posted and some fifty-three men went back to the camp under the same old conditions, but this did not break the strike. On the 1st of February there appeared a notice in the "Chapleau Rost" that we remaining' strikers had been finally dismissed, and our names struck from the books of Austin and Nicholson, and that our places had been fi!led.	.
Lp to this time relief had been refused by the district relief officer on the grounds that there were still our old jobs open to us in the camps. On February 5th outside union assistance failed entirely and we were faced with starvation, so once again we approached the relief officer and he informed us that he had written the department in Toronto stating that we were no longer in the vicinity and that was the information they had to go by in Toronto, but I was able to inform Mr. Wo'fe that [ had taken a precaution against this by sending the Hon. Charles McCrea. representative of Sudbury district, the information by telegram on February 2nd that two hundred men were still on strike in Chapleau. destitute and forced to seek relief owing to their jobs being taken by strikebreakers shipped in from Quebec and that they had my information in Toronto to counteract h?s. He had sent in his report without consulting us, the principals, and his report was erroneous so we asked him to send in a true report and obtain the relief

Relief Act, 1934
to which we were entitled and which, in the face of starvation, was so sorely needed. Mr. Wolfe's voice failed him so that he was unable to phone the proper authorities. The sergeant of the provincial police took up our case in conjunction with the mayor of Chapleau, and as a result we were able to secure enough emergency supplies to carry us till the next dey. On the following day, February 6, Mr. Wolfe, the relief officer, was confined to bed and we were faced with a worse situation than before. for the relief officer could not be seen. Therefore I deemed it expedient to send the following telegram to Hon. Charles McCrea, to the Minister of Labour and also the Minister of Lands and Forests; "Bushmen still d statute in Chapleau. Situation critical. Relief formally app'ied for several days aeo. No action. District Relief Officer T. H. Wolfe sick abed to-day. Who is responsible? Reply at once." The following reply came back from Dr. Robb. February 7. 1934: "Relief officer Mr. Wolfe will handle your situation."
On presenting this telegram to Mr. Wolfe at his bedside he stated that anything he might do would relieve the situation till the next morning only. He asked me to leave the town at once, and stated that if the strikers broke down the organization he would deal with them individually and have them come in to him one by one. My reply was that I had been elected by the men to present their case for relief on their behalf, and that our intentions were to remain organized for the mutual benefit of all concerned. Since then Mr. Wolfe has remained confined to the house, and the provincial police have been handling the relief situation and procuring supplies for us, quite to the satisfaction of all of us. Mayor Edwards, on being approached as to whether the relief officer had any authority to ask me to leave town, stated that Mr. Wolfe had no authority to make the request, and the town council said they appreciated the value of our organized efforts in preventing trouble and extended to me their hearty cooperation and the freedom of the town. The provincial police came in on this strike, prepared to fight, but remained to play, so to speak, and they also appreciate the value of organized unity. As citizens we recognize the rights of others and only expect that our similar rights be respected in turn. The Minister of Lands and Forests asked to be advised of the number of men who desired to go to board camps, so we held another meeting and took a census of 130 destitute strikers, who all wished to remain in Chapleau as a unit, to press their claim to the proper government authorities in Toronto and Ottawa for a full investigation into the present existing conditions in the lumber camps, and also investigate discrepancies in the expenditure of the taxpayers" money for relief in the unorganized districts in the vicinity of Chapleau. The men appointed me, by election, at the meeting, to present the case on their behalf to the proper official authorities. The following telegram was therefore sent to Mr. Finlayson, the Minister of Lands and Forests, in reply to his. February 7. 1934: "Your wire received. Mr. Wolfe states that anything he might do will relieve situation until to-morrow morning only. Approximately one hundred and thirty men destitute and willing to work for relief here until strike settled, but require immediate and impartial inquiry into industrial dispute here. The situation is extremely critical to-night. Wire advice." The same wire was also sent to the Minister of Labour, Toronto, on that day, February 7, when the affair was also laid before the federal Minister of Labour, as you ha to confirmed. Our meeting was no communist affair, as some people in town have been led to believe, for there were two or three provincial police present at the meeting who were quite prepared to handle any eventuality of that sort. We are a lumber workers' organization. Nicholson says that our funds are backed from Moscow but we haven't seen any " Moscow gold " as yet nor do we expect to require it.
G. B. Nicholson made the statement from the public platform on the occasion of his meeting here on January 22nd that his camps conformed to the relief standards as to sanitary conditions. That is one point to be settled before the investigation committee which we require here, as to whether Nicholson's camps are relief camps or lumber camps. If the operation of the Austin & Nicholson Lumber Company is being assisted from the relief funds of the province and dominion, well it is a scandalous misuse of the taxpayers' money which will precipitate one of the biggest investigations in the north country. The district sanitary inspector, I). S. McKee of Sudbury made an aeroplane trip into the camps in the company of G. B. Nicholson, on a tour of inspection, after the strikers had left the camps. Consequently there appeared in the press an account of McKee's report as to sanitary conditions in the camps. This report I brand as false and have endeavoured to have the Ottawa Citizen publish a letter in our defence, for we made no unjustified complaints as to existing sanitary conditions in the camps.
There are three very good reasons why this Chapleau strike should be a federal issue.
1.	G. B. Nicholson represented the lumber men of Canada at the imperial conference in Ottawa last summer, and while there, I believe, a great fuss was made about Great Britain trading with countries that employed slave labour and had uncivilized living conditions. Well, this is the very mess which we have laid on Mr. Nicholson's doorstep here in Chapleau, and we are of the opinion that the cleaning-up should begin here at home.
2.	The corrupt method of breaking our lawful strike, by bringing in strikebreakers from the province of Quebec, to take our jobs in Ontario, is surely an interprovincial affair, to be investigated best by the federal government.
3.	As a direct result of the unscrupulous methods of strikebreaking used by Mr. Nicholson, we are forced to draw on relief funds which, in our case, I expect are 50 per cent federal and 50 per cent provincial, as we are from an unorganized district.
Those are the reasons, fairly put, why we require an industrial investigation, as provided already in the present session of parliament. The investigation should cover, in this Chapleau district, the lumber camps, sanitary conditions, workmen's compensation for bushmen. and the relief scandal that evidently exists here.
Our men intend to remain here as witnesses on their own behalf for the investigation
The time is now opportune to draft a clean labour code for the north, and the north is worthy of it, for we are now on the threshhold
Relief Act, 1934

of unprecedented development of natural resources in this district, as the mineral possibilities here are being probed deeply these days.
The situation here requires an investigation committee that will be able to investigate anything from a member of parliament's collar to the Royal Bank. At any rate, it will disclose present graft and corruption which dissipates the taxpayers' sweat-earned contribution to civilization. It is only fair to our imperial trade relations that such an abject condition here should be wiped out, for Britain has ever been averse to slavery, especially in 1934, when we should be marching onward rather than reverting to customs of the dark ages.

Personally, I am a Canadian citizen of British pioneer stock, born, reared and schooled in Bromley township, Renfrew county till January 1, 1927. when I came to the unorganized districts in the vicinity of Chapleau, where I have made my living since as bushman, track-worker, sawmill hand, river driver, trapper and prospector. At present I am a property holder in Sudbury district, as I hold a number of mining claims in the Swayze gold area, near here.
Strikers here want only a living wage and civilized living conditions. It is not our fault that the strike is still on, as we have done everything in our power to reach a settlement long ago. We were forced to seek relief as our jobs were filled by outsiders.

There is nothing further from my mind than the belief that by any act or word of mine I could stampede this committee into any hurried action on anything. In regard to this legislation and the legislation passed last year, the government must table each day the orders in council passed thereunder. Each act reflected by an order in council under the legislation of last year was laid on the table of the house for the information of hon. members, as the records will shew. I should like to add to what I have just said that this long delay in introducing this measure this session, resulting in the legislation coming up just before an adjournment of parliament, is part of a deliberate policy on the part of the administration to put off at every session until the last moment any discussion with reference to labour matters. It was the same at the special session of 1930; very little time was given for the discussion of labour matters and all the time was taken up with questions of the tariff and national revenue. In the 1931 session the legislation was brought down in the very closing days of the session. It was the same during the following session; if one looks at the records I cited the other night it will be found that the deliberate attempt of the government with respect to this question of unemployment has been to delay until the last moment and then to try to crowd the legislation through because of some adjournment or because of prorogation. I think the minister will find that in 1934 he can do all that he did in 1932, with respect to these matters, notwithstanding that an adjournment may intervene. I think he will find himself able to do all that is necessary in the matter of meeting the situation.

I heard the hon. member
himself read one the other day; he read one from the Unity league, from a man named Davis.

I may read one today and when I do I will tell the committee just who Davis is. However, having failed in the impression which he has tried to convey to this house and to the country at large- and the newspapers commented on the fact that the hon. member for North Timiskaming had been in the camps in the Chapleau area, and I have read Hansard myself-what does the hon. gentleman do? He reads a series of documents written by a paid agent of the labour defence league, which operates under divers hames in northern Ontario, these documents bearing the name of a man named Connolly whom I have known for years. His signature appears on these documents, or is authorized to appear thereon, and this man Connolly boasts openly that he is being paid $-1 a day with expenses for doing the work he is now engaged in. I can prove that he so boasts. When his fellow workers were going back to the woods, after having been brought out under false pretences by six communists who went to get them, Connolly stated to his fellow workers, "Why should I worry? Why should I go back to the woods when I am getting S4 a day for what I am doing?" If my hon. friend will go to the bottom of this matter he will find that it is just these communist organizations that are endeavouring to ensnare and entrap honest Canadian workmen. I will say frankly that Connolly was an honest working man, a good type of Canadian citizen without question, as are all the other men working there; but the fact is'that they have allowed themselves to be led into this trap.
Let me mention one other matter to which my hon. friend refers. The letter which he read made the statement that Nicholson was a member of the lumbermen's committee at the Ottawa conference. Well, I admit the accusation; I was a member of that committee, it having been my honour to have been selected as chairman. And let me say to you, Mr. Chairman, that it was because of the effort made by that committee, and the success it achieved, with the support of this government, in getting Canadian lumber into
the United Kingdom market that this attack is made on the industry not only in northern Ontario but as well in northwestern Quebec.
There has been organized in northern Ontario a group of Canadians, honest, earnest Canadian citizens of all nationalities, known as the Canadian Bushmen's Union. They are registered under the Trade Unions Act. In this regard, I wish to repeat what I said on a previous occasion. So far as I am concerned, I will do everything which it is humanly possible for any man to do, and to-day I am actively engaged, with other Canadian lumbermen, in an effort to bring about a condition whereby woodsmen operating in the Canadian provinces will be drawn together in a regularly constituted body of organized labour in which collective bargaining will be possible. It is not possible under present circumstances, and if my hon. friend will only survey conditions in his own riding he will realize that fact. Now what do these budimen say? Writing to the Minister of Labour they make this statement:
Press dispatches state that you informed the House of Commons on Friday last, the strike at Chapleau. Ontario, had been organized by the Canadian Labour Defence League according to information in your department. Another dispatch from Toronto quotes Rev. A. E. Smith as stating you were in error in making this claim. Rev. Smith claims that: "The league had nothing to do with that strike except to defend those who may be arrested."
Well, the defence of one arrested was not successful because he is back in gaol, out of which he broke in order to participate in these labour difficulties. The letter goes on:
This organization, the Canadian Bushmen's Union, registered under the Trade Unions Act, wishes to emphatically endorse the statement you made.
As the result of intense communistic activities in the timber industry, and the endless upheavals causing heavy losses to the workers ns well as subjecting them to constant agitation, the Canadian-minded workers determined to organize on the same basis as other Canadian labour unions. Close to six hundred men have joined the movement, which started the latter part of December.
We have plenty of evidence that the Canadian Labour Defence League is part and parcel of the general communistic move in Canada,-
Everyone who has endeavoured to ascertain the facts knows this to be true.
-which includes eighteen or more organizations. I have just rec.eived information that if the Conviction of Rev. Smith should result in the C.L.D.L. being outlawed, that the United Labour Farmers' Temple Association will immediately take over the activities of the C.L.D.L.
And so on. This organization makes other statements. It has been checking up on the labour defence league all through.

Relief Act, 1934

Over a period of years the timber and other basic industries and their labour have been harassed and penalized by the intolerant boorish and fanatical agitation of foreign semi-political organizations. And' all business, and labour dependent more or less on the industries affected, have suffered severe losses.
They realize that by reason of the fact that the labour difficulty in the Port Arthur district compelled pulpwood purchasers for the United States to go elsewhere for their products, between fifteen hundred and two thousand men were idle in that district this winter-men who otherwise would have been at work. The whole thing is a carefully planned scheme to prevent the forest products industry from continuing in successful operation in Canada. That is the whole point.
There are one or two other matters which I would refer to. My hon. friend, in reading from that letter which we have heard, took responsibility for it, and the letter stated that the operations in the Chapleau area were being assisted by relief funds. Let me say, Mr. Chairman, that that statement is subject to one of two interpretations: Either it is a statement made without any knowledge whatever of the facts, or there was deliberate intention to mislead this committee and this country. No such thing has ever existed. The same applies to what I referred to on Monday night with regard to reduction on crown dues. No reduction was made on crown dues after these lumber difficulties occurred. It was agreed last year with the operators, the pulpwood companies and everyone else in New Brunswick. Nova Scotia, the provinces of Quebec, Ontario and British Columbia that as a means of getting men back into the woods a reduction would be made in crown dues and stumpage. Every contract that was made either for logs or for pulpwood was based on that understanding, the increment arising from the reduction in dues being payable to the contracting firm or company, and the contractor having nothing to do with it. The question of wages was not included.
My hon. friend poses as an advocate of fair play and decent wages for woodsmen. He made the statement, in reading, that wages in these camps were from $15 to S26 per month. I say to this committee that the minimum wage paid in any one of these camps was S2G per month and up. The system of piece work has been followed in the lumbering industry of this country ever since I have known anything about it, because the men want piece work; they want an opportunity of working when they are in the woods and of deriving the advantage arising there-

from. I can say that there are men who are earning $100 a month and board on piece work.
My hon. friend makes another statement. He says that G. B. Nicholson went to Toronto, when this difficulty occurred, to interview the attorney general and the head of the provincial police. I say to him again that that is another statement either based on lack of knowledge or made with intent to deceive. G. B. Nicholson did nothing of the kind. He was in Toronto on a business trip when he received the telegram that some of the men were coming out of the woods. As I stated on Monday night, he immediately returned to his office in Chapleau and went into the woods to see what the difficulty was. My hon. friend stated that 400 men came out of those camps. I state to him now that 400 men did not come out of the camps. There were 561 men in the eight camps affected and 228 came out, leaving 333 in the camps.
The statement is again made that men were put into those camps under a heavy police guard. As occurs in every case in this province, in Iroquois Falls, Cochrane, Smooth Rock Falls and Kapuskasing, as soon as trouble develops wherever it may happen, the authorities take the precaution, on the request of the local police, to get some men in to see that peace is maintained. That is all there is to that. The men went through of their own volition; they were going all the time. Let me repeat what I said before: This trouble did not begin in January; it was not a strike in any sense whatever; it was just a continuation of men being agitated, disturbed and persuaded on a variety of pleas to leave their employment.
As regards the men who caused the trouble, my hon. friend says that they were not communists. Well, they demonstrated the fact that they were not very honest men in the first instance by going to an employment agent and hiring as pulpwood cutters, whereas not one of them, as they admitted, had ever cut a stick in his life before. Six of them hired under these names: MoMaster, Riley, alias Davis, alias Dacko, operating on the Transcontinental line in the Kapuskasing district under the last name; Doyle, alias Berry-and both of them ex-convicts sent there by the people financing Vapaus, the communist organ in the city of Sudbury- Menekin and Makela.
My hon. friend says that employees of Austin-Nicholson or Brownlee presented a demand for a change in conditions and an increase in wages. No employee of Austin-

Nicholson ever presented a demand or a request for any changed conditions whatever until exactly one week from the day the men were induced to come out at Chapleau, three of them, Wright, Connolly and St. Michel, came to see me. I saw them, talked with them and stated exactly what we would do; I said: "There are the conditions; if you want to work, you are quite welcome." We kept the offer open for three long weeks and the 128 of the 228, leaving 100 all told-and a large number of them had gone to their homes in the meantime-went back to their work inside of ten days, glad to get the opportunity. They came to my house on the Monday evening, asking me how they could get on the train and out to their work without being molested by this communist organization. I undertook to look after them and they went back to work.
My hon. friend says that these men were destitute. Let me tell the committee exactly how destitute they were. Of the 228 that came out, 142 took settlements from the clerks in the camps and there was distributed amongst them in cash the sum of $6,000 odd for the time that they had worked in the woods. Forty of them never went near the camps before they came out. They were advised by Messrs. Davis, Daeko, etcetera, etcetera:	Do not take your time; just leave
what is coming to you there, and they walked out, some of them leaving their clothes behind them, under a promise that they would be paid $5 a day if they remained out in order to do what? Just as Mr. Berry, who is now in gaol, stated publicly in the town of Chapleau, their purpose was to destroy this industry and to make it impossible to carry it on.
It is approaching six o'clock. I do not know that I can add anything else except to say that as regards the men who came out, leaving their time behind them, there was still
83,000	due to them which was sent to them just as soon as we were able to find out where they were. My hon. friend says that there are still 200 strikers in Chapleau. He can send anyone there he likes and he cannot find amongst them ten men who have ever worked in those camps in their lives.
Let me in conclusion make this observation with regard to the letters. I have under my hand similar letters and I know the man who is writing them. Because of the sympathy I have for the poor fellow's family I am not going to say who he is although I may be forced to do so if my hon. friend continues the campaign he has undertaken to wage against me and the organization I 74726-1225
happen to represent. The letters are being written by a man who is being paid to write them and he is being paid by the communist organ known as Vapaus published at Sudbury. That covers part of the situation. I could spend the whole night reading documents that I have under my hand, to prove just what the situation is.
